answer:
WHO's World Malaria Report 2024 found that malaria's global toll rose again in 2023:

263 million cases and 597,000 deaths were estimated worldwide in 2023—about 11 million more cases than in 2022, while deaths remained nearly unchanged. [1]
The WHO African Region bore the overwhelming burden: about 95% of malaria deaths occurred there. [1]
Progress since 2000 has been substantial: malaria control efforts are estimated to have averted 2.2 billion cases and 12.7 million deaths. But recent trends show that gains are not enough to meet global targets. [1]
The report highlighted unequal access to prevention, diagnosis and treatment. It called for more inclusive services for groups at higher risk or facing barriers to care, including young children, women and girls, Indigenous Peoples, migrants, people with disabilities, and people in remote areas. [1]
WHO emphasized that reversing the trend will require broader access to effective tools and stronger efforts to reach underserved communities. [1]

In short, the report showed both major long-term progress and a worrying recent rise in cases, with the heaviest burden falling on communities with the least access to care.
